en: *The Explanatory Commentary on the Meaning of the Dharma-Gate of the Secret Mind-Ground of the Mahāyoga of the Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
This yoga sūtra is divided into two major sections: first, the verses summarizing the general characteristics and offering praise; second, the long [prose exposition].
Regarding the practice of benefiting oneself and others through conduct and so forth, it is further divided into two parts within the verses:

first, one should know that the four lines of the initial verse constitute a general taking of refuge in the Triple Gem; secondly, the subsequent section constitutes the specific taking of refuge in the Noble Assembly.
This section is further divided into two parts:
first, ten lines of homage to the Tathāgatas of the Five Families; second, ten lines of homage to the four Great Bodhisattvas.

Within the initial ten lines, the four lines beginning with "Vajra-body, speech, and mind" pay homage to and praise Vairocana Buddha; the subsequent six lines beginning with "The heroic and fierce Akṣobhya" should be understood as paying homage to the Tathāgatas of the four directions.

The final ten phrases dedicate the merit to the four great Bodhisattvas. Among them, the first two phrases praise and pay homage to Vajragarbha Bodhisattva; the next two phrases praise and pay homage to Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva; the third pair of phrases praise and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; the fourth pair of phrases praise and pay homage to Viśvakarman Bodhisattva; and the fifth pair of phrases should be understood as concluding the virtues and dedicating them collectively.

These two preceding lines and so forth were placed at the beginning of the sutra by the great ācāryas who compiled the *Yogācārabhūmi* in the West, as they first offered praise and homage using its preeminent characteristics. It should be understood that at the head of all such sutras, a verse of praise and homage is invariably established according to that tradition; however, the former sages of this land [China] omitted it and did not translate it.
Next, I shall now set forth the titles of the scriptures based on forty characters in total from works such as the *Vajraśekhara* in one hundred thousand verses.

There exists a broad version of this scripture consisting of one hundred thousand verses, which has not been heard of in this land; it is entirely the realm of the profound secrets of all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas, and is not something that can be heard or known by those of small wisdom, such as Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, humans, or devas.

These two fascicles of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* herein present a shallow and abbreviated version of the practices derived from this scripture; as for its extensive details, the faculties [of those here] are not yet capable of bearing them.

This is the *Yogācāryabhūmi-saṃgraha*; in the Western lands (India), those who have received empowerment transmit it through oral instruction and formal entrustment, yet even its extensive version has not been passed down here.
Furthermore, the version in one hundred thousand stanzas is itself a secondary abridgment from within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Regarding the original text of that great sūtra, the Ācārya said that its volume was as wide and long as a bed and four or five feet thick; it contained immeasurable verses and was kept within an iron stūpa in the region of South India.
During the several hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, no one was able to open this stūpa, as it had been sealed with iron doors and iron locks.

At that time, the Buddha-dharma was gradually declining in the land of India. There was once a great virtuous one who had previously recited and upheld the mantra of Mahāvairocana; he attained the manifestation of Mahāvairocana Buddha’s body and his many emanations, who then spoke this dharma-gate along with its words and phrases from within the void. Having caused them to be transcribed in their proper sequence, they immediately vanished—this is the present single fascicle of the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-japa-vidhi*.

At that time, this Great Virtuous One, having achieved mastery through recitation, made a vow to open this stūpa; he circumambulated the stūpa while reciting for seven days, and by striking the door of the stūpa with seven grains of white mustard seed, it opened.

The deities within the stupa simultaneously became enraged and would not allow him to enter; he could only see from within the stupa the light of incense and lamps extending for one or two zhang, with famous flowers and precious canopies suspended and arranged throughout its interior, and he also heard voices of praise extolling this King of Sutras.
At that time, this Great Virtuous One repented with a sincere heart and made a great vow; only then was he permitted to enter the stūpa. Once he had entered, the stūpa immediately closed.

After reciting this extensive version of the King of Sūtras once over many days, it took him no more than the duration of a meal. Having received the instructions of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas regarding what he was capable of, he was able to memorize it without forgetting. He was then ordered to leave the stūpa, whereupon the gate closed as before.
At that time, the Dharma recorded and upheld in writing consisted of one hundred thousand verses.
As for this scripture titled the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*, its extensive version within the Great Treasury Stūpa of the Bodhisattvas is beyond compare in this world.
The light within the stupa remains as bright as ever even to this day and has not been extinguished. A version of this sutra in one hundred thousand verses does not yet exist in this country.
Regarding the arrival of this abridged version in our land, at the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi said:
"When I set out from the Western Regions and crossed the South Sea, there were more than thirty large ships, each carrying five or six hundred people, all crossing the great ocean together at once."
While traveling upon the sea, he encountered a great storm; all the ships and their occupants were swept away and submerged, and the ship he was aboard was likewise on the verge of sinking.

At that time, the two sets of the *Sūtra-vastu* (the longer versions) were always kept near his person, maintained and venerated by him. When the captain saw the ship about to sink, he cast all the goods on board into the sea; in his state of panic, he forgot to retrieve the *sūtra-vastu* bundles. Consequently, the version in one hundred thousand stanzas was also cast into the sea, leaving only the abridged version remaining.

At that time, I resolved to perform a rite for the removal of calamities; immediately, the great wind ceased, and for a distance of more than one *li* around the ship, neither the wind nor the waves stirred.
All those on board came to me for refuge, and we gradually set sail, reaching this shore and arriving in this country.

In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, Master Xingyi came to the Western Capital and requested from me the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Having heard of this extraordinary and rare Dharma-gate, he commissioned Yiśvara to translate it into Chinese; Xingyi and others personally acted as scribes, recording it strictly according to the sequence of the Sanskrit original. While the meaning was not lost, the phrasing and syntax were not yet fully perfected.

"Observing this with my own eyes, even those practitioners who have studied it extensively do not know where to begin, and for those of shallow wisdom and dull intellect, it is likewise difficult to enter.

Now, having received the intent of the teachings and transmitted them, I have somewhat grasped their essence; the secret meaning resides largely within the words themselves. As the Dharma spreads, I have forcefully opened up expedient means and analytical gates to mark its ultimate destination."
Within this very sūtra’s prose section on the practice of benefiting oneself and others, it is further divided into two parts.

First, from the passage beginning with "If a practitioner... down to "...having completed the yoga practice and the formal cross-legged posture," is the general gate; it constitutes the secret adornment of internally realized great wisdom, wherein one sees the accomplishment of phenomena and attains the state of a Tathāgata—this is the benefit for oneself.

From the second section, "Cultivating Yoga," down to the end of the sutra, one has already entered the general gateway; the purpose is to skillfully establish the characteristics of secret wisdom, to gather sentient beings and lead them into the state of Buddhahood—this is the practice of benefiting others.
This may also be understood as a single section, as both [the preceding and following parts] equally possess the practice of benefiting oneself and others.
Within the previous section on benefiting oneself, it is further divided into three parts:

first, from the beginning up to "or when a great bodhisattva has sat in the full-lotus posture" and continuing through "performing them according to one's inclination," this constitutes the method for purifying karmic obstructions through the three types of action and the four modes of deportment.

The second section, from "The practitioner desires to purify himself" down to "further reflecting upon the secret mantra he holds," constitutes the Dharma of the Seal of Wisdom of the True Reality, the realm of all Buddhas, which is the gateway to the samādhi of entering wisdom.

The third section, from "further reflecting upon" down to "having practiced yoga," constitutes the Dharma of merging delusion into wisdom to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment and abide in great bodhi.
Regarding the first section, a verse is spoken:
Teacher and disciple together receive and practice; Gathering, guiding, and exhorting to cultivate the Dharma;
Next, the initial arising, practice, and abiding; The methods of the gate of speech through empowerment.
The methods for washing the face and chewing the tooth-stick; The methods for relieving oneself and binding the protective dharma;
The methods for rinsing the mouth and bathing; And the methods for bathing the honored deities of the division;
Visualizing the adornment of the body internally and externally; Next, the methods for entering the maṇḍala.
The methods for universal prostration and repentance with directional orientation, the specific dedication of offerings and vows,
the four modes of conduct according to one's inclination, and the methods for removing, increasing, subduing, and destroying [obstacles]. Regarding the first section,
the methods for the teacher and disciple to jointly practice and encourage cultivation, there are six parts herein:
The first instruction on selecting the vessel is found in the sutra from "If one practices up to the rites of homa," etc.
The second, the benefit of generating the resolve, is found in the sutra from "O Vajra disciple, up to all sinful obstructions shall be extinguished," etc.

The third is the inclusion of wrong views, which refers to the passage in the sutra beginning with, "There may be sentient beings who enter deeply [into the path] for the sake of departing from the evil destinies," and so forth.

The fourth is the encouragement to practice for the sake of obtaining benefits, which refers to the passage in the sutra beginning with, "If a son of good family... up to what is sought," and so forth.

The fifth concerns the entrustment to those who are worthy; this is found in the sutra from the passage beginning, "If a Vajrācārya sees someone with sincere faith, he should cause them to resolve their mind," and so forth.

The sixth concerns the indication of dwelling in an excellent location; this is found in the sutra from the passage beginning, "The place for performing the ritual should be on superior ground... practicing according to the Dharma," and so forth.
These six sections have been explained extensively; fearing prolixity, they shall not be detailed here—this should be understood.

Regarding the verse on "the initial arising of the method for abiding in practice," the Sūtra states: "Whenever a practitioner of yoga sleeps, and so forth, up to 'should extensively benefit all sentient beings,'" etc.; this is called the method of initial arising.
The commentary states:

This means that a practitioner of yoga should constantly perceive their own body as the Vairocana-Vajra body. When sleeping or resting, they should imagine entering the Vajra-samādhi; that is, with the mind tranquil as if having entered nirvāṇa, they should visualize themselves as the seal-mark (*mudrā*) of the five wisdoms, surrounded by blazing flames, and only then sleep according to their will. This is called the "corresponding visualization of the body-samādhi."
When arising, one should conceive of arising from the Vajra-samādhi; therefore, this secret meaning is called "Vajra-arising.
*Vajra* is the name for the characteristic of the Vajra-samādhi.
*Tiṣṭha* means "to arise" or "to be established.
*Oṃ* is the crown of the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas.
This is a secret teaching, and its sublime visualization is transmitted solely through oral instruction.

This mudrā is named Vajrasamādhi; Vajrasamādhi is called the Awakened One (Buddha). It causes one to contemplate the meaning of the gāthā by understanding that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure and free from self-nature, yet undergoes various transformations driven by karma.
Having understood this meaning, one practices beneficial conduct; thus it is said, "one should extensively benefit others," and so forth.
The Sūtra states, "If one gives rise to the desire for practice and mantras," and so on; this is called the method of practice.
The commentary states:
This refers to the practice of samādhi.
Its esoteric meaning is the "stride of the vajra-samādhi."
The Sūtra states: "If one abides in this place and in the mantras and so forth, this is called the dharma of abiding.
The commentary explains:
"The secret meaning is to abide in the Vajra-samādhi."
The meaning of *Oṃ* is as explained above; the subsequent instances should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the verse "the method for empowering the gateway of speech," the Sūtra states: "Desiring to speak with others, whether in ordinary language or through mantras," and so forth.
The commentary states:

One places the syllable RAṂ, representing the mind of the dharma-realm, upon the tip of the tongue; one visualizes it emitting various kinds of light, and further empowers the sounds of speech with the mantra.
If this refers to the secret meaning of the sages, it is the sound of the holy power of the Vajra-samādhi.

As for the verse stating "washing the face and chewing the tooth-stick," the Sūtra says: "When washing the face, as well as when reciting mantras, one should give rise to joy in all things," and so forth.
The commentary states:
This water is produced from the Vajrasamādhi; by using it to wash one’s face, the face becomes like a vajra, such that no māras dare to look directly upon it, and all Tathāgatas are filled with joy.

Next, regarding the method for chewing the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), the Sūtra states: "When chewing the willow branch (*yāñzhī*), one should do so after performing the empowerment (*adhitiṣṭhati*)," and so forth.
The commentary explains:
If one performs this according to the Dharma, it can cause the practitioner to achieve the Vajra-Smile Samādhi; therefore, the secret meaning refers to the virtues of the Buddha.
Through the empowerment of the Vajra-laughter Samādhi, it is said that one is able to destroy all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
As for forming the vajra-fist with the "feather" [of the index finger], it consists of grasping the tooth-stick firmly with the right hand while holding the thumb.

Regarding the verse that says, “The dharma for easily performing the binding protection,” the Sūtra states: “If one wishes to go to a place where it is convenient, one should immediately form the armor-seal (*kavaca-mudrā*) with both hands, and so forth, until the ritual of purification has been completed.”
The commentary states:
This sutra lacks the seal (mudrā) of the adamantine armor; it is now described here. As for the armor seal:

first, join the two hands in *añjali* at the heart; then, place the two index fingers along the backs of the two middle fingers, and hold the two thumbs side-by-side upright, pressing against the joints of the middle phalanges of the two middle fingers—this is it.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajrakavaca hūṃ. Regarding the secret meaning: one is empowered by donning the armor of the Buddha-virtue Vajra-samādhi.
With this secret mantra-seal, seal the two shoulders, the left and right flanks, the waist, the thighs, and so forth of the body, visualizing oneself as being clad in armor.
Again, place the seal upon the crown of the head, forming two vajra-fists respectively.
As for the fist: each of the four fingers from the index finger downward grasps the thumb.
Placing the fists together at the crown of the head, one should extend the two index fingers straight upward like the points of needles, their tips touching, and visualize them as the "head-peak."

Again, separate the two hands at the shoulders and bring them down to the heart; join the tips of the index fingers together. Then, apply the syllables OṂ KṢOṂ HŪṂ to the two index fingers and visualize the two index fingers emitting five-colored light that forms a vajra-girdle. Subsequently, it encircles the body from top to bottom like the fastening of armor. This is called the method for adorning with armor, as described in the sūtra.

Next, one consecrates the site and again abides in the *dharmadhātu-citta*. With the two Vajra-protectors on the left and right—namely, this three-syllable protection of the body—one emits great flames of light that blaze forth intensely outward.
Furthermore, one should employ empowerment by means of the vidyā-mudrā; as the mudrā-form is described in the sūtra, it is said that all evils belonging to the three realms are thereby extinguished.
If one is unable to employ the aforementioned vidyā-mudrā, one may also achieve the same result by reciting only the subsequent universal secret vidyā-mantra.
If both are employed together, the *śāntika* (pacifying) rite is superior.
One should know that for all subsequent mantras, one should employ the aforementioned mudrā; it should be used everywhere to perform binding and protection (*rakṣā*).
Regarding the verse on "the method of bathing at the mouth," the Sūtra states: "With this secret vidyā, empower the vajra-water and recite the mantra until it reaches the mouth," and so forth.
The commentary states:

Regarding the secret meaning, the Vajra Samādhi of the Buddha’s Virtue and Great Compassion purifies the impurities of speech with its water, causing the karma of speech to become pure and opening the gateway of quiescent wisdom; this is called the Dharma of Purifying Speech.
Next, regarding the method for bathing, the Sūtra states: "One should then bathe. There are four kinds of bathing; one may perform them daily as desired, or according to one's capacity. And so forth.
The commentary states:
First, "possessing the three types of discipline" means causing one to abide in the three samādhis and manifesting the three bodies.
Second, "prostrating, repenting, and confessing" means purifying karmic obstructions and attaining unimpeded wisdom.
Third, regarding the words for the offering of mudrās: this is to cause all Buddhas to rejoice and to increase one's merit and lifespan.
Fourth, bathing with scented water: this is to make the limbs supple and to accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Practicing in accordance with this is the meaning of "bathing"; it can be understood by reflecting upon it.
The meaning of the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*) is explained in detail in other sūtras.

Regarding the verse line "along with the bathing ritual for the honored deities," the sūtra states: "When entering a pool of water to bathe, first visualize it as a pond that delights the devas; in the center of the water, visualize the most supreme and sublime maṇḍala-wheel of the Tathāgata, and so forth, until you visualize that entire wheel-maṇḍala entering into your own body. Etc.
The commentary states:

One visualizes the five syllables and so forth as seeds, from which arise the various assemblies of honored ones belonging to each respective family; one then offers worship by filling the hollows of both hands with scented water and so forth.
Regarding the method for scooping water, the scripture does not explain it in full detail; I shall now describe it completely.

First, place both hands side-by-side with the palms turned downward as if holding an object, and insert the two thumbs into the hollow formed by the hands. Scoop up the water three times and direct it outward toward the honored one. Visualize that the water is poured over each part of the honored one’s form individually, or visualize bathing them all at once. The remainder of the text is easily understood.

The verse states, "Visualizing the adornment of the body, both internally and externally. The Sūtra says, "Having visualized in this manner, one emerges and stands upon the shore... [and so forth] up to the secret mantra and the true meaning of the principles," and so on.
The commentary states:
Regarding "always wearing a girdle," this refers to one's personal adornment.
Furthermore, as for adorning the body with head-crowns and the like, there is no such seal (mudrā) in the sūtra; it is now described here once more.

With both hands, cross them outward with the right over the left; join the tips of the two middle fingers like lotus petals and place them upon the crown of the head. Then, forming vajra-fists, separate the hands from the two sides of the head and let them descend along the body, visualizing them as becoming hair-bands, celestial garments, and so forth.
When forming the mudrā, recite this mantra:
Oṃ vajrapadma mahāviśodhaka samantavajri. As for the secret meaning: it signifies that the Buddha-virtue Vajra-lotus crown is placed upon the crown of my head.

Having performed these rites, one should, according to one’s inclination, visualize oneself as one body with the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Then, one should visualize holding a *vajra* and so forth, up to the secret mantras (*vidyā*) and the true meaning of their principles, reflecting upon these according to what one personally maintains.
The remaining text is easily understood.

Regarding the verse that says, "Next, the method for entering the maṇḍala," the Sūtra states: "Thereafter, when one is about to go to and enter the maṇḍala site... up until 'dispelling all inauspiciousness,' etc."
The commentary states:
This is the aforementioned *mukha* (face) mantra.

Regarding the "binding of the *vajra-muṣṭi* (vajra-fist)": clench the left hand into a fist by grasping the thumb, while simultaneously producing the *vajra-śabda* (vajra-sound); with this fist, one opens the door to make it wide open.
Regarding "the eyes of wrath," this refers to looking sideways to the left and right with the pupils of the compassionate heart fully round.

As for the verse stating "universally prostrating and repenting while facing [all directions]," the Sūtra says: "Having entered, one maintains right mindfulness toward the ten directions of the eternally abiding [Buddhas], and so forth, until having performed the rites according to the Dharma."
The commentary states:
At the beginning of this practice, one should universally imagine paying homage to the eternally abiding assembly of Vairocana’s Dharma-realm.
This [rite] should include the practices of repentance, exhortation, sympathetic joy, and dedication; any omissions therein are for the sake of brevity.
The practitioner of yoga constantly abides in the vajra body, speech, and mind; that is, they revolve into the body of Samantabhadra’s all-pervading vows and conduct.
Because this dharma is complete, it is not set forth in detail here; those who desire it may practice it as they wish.
The prostration with the five limbs and kneeling can be understood from the context.

Regarding the verse that says, "The specific method for returning and offering vows," the Sūtra states: "Immediately rising from one's seat, again placing the right knee upon the ground, and so forth, performing the ritual as described above by facing the four directions, and having completed the prostrations," and so on.
The commentary states:
This has four meanings.
First, it is for the sake of accomplishing the stage of the universal conduct of Vajrasattva Samantabhadra of all Buddhas.
Second, for the sake of fulfilling the stage of the vajra consecration of all Buddhas;
third, for the sake of swiftly bringing about the accomplishment of the stage of all Tathāgatas turning the wheel of Dharma;
and fourth, for the sake of equally attaining the skillful activities of all Tathāgatas.
Regarding these four types of samādhi, one may enter them simultaneously, sequentially, or enter one according to one's preference.
Whenever they are performed, one must first form the initial Vajrasamaya mudrā, and subsequently join the palms to pay homage in the respective directions.
Regarding the secret meaning of the mantra: it refers to the supreme Vajra-samādhi of the Buddha’s virtues; therefore, one should first form the mudrā as described in the sūtra.
The passages concerning "respectful prostrations" and so forth can be understood from the text.
Regarding the desire to enter the four types of samādhi gates, there is first a general enumeration, followed by a detailed listing.
The sūtra’s passage, "Furthermore, one should personally perform a single prostration to each," etc., constitutes the general enumeration; its meaning is readily understandable.

Regarding the first, the Vajra Samantabhadra Samādhi, the Sūtra states: "In the eastern direction, prostrating with the entire body on the ground, [reciting] the mantra, and so forth, up to 'gracious empowerment' (*anugraha*)," and so on.
The commentary states:

As for its secret meaning, one should visualize that throughout the entire realm of space in the eastern direction, it is purely adorned with vajras; this is called the world-system named Vajravyūhagarbha.
Within that space, Tathāgatas filled the world-systems, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds.
Each and every Tathāgata entered the Vajra-samādhi, sat cross-legged, extended his right hand down over his right knee, and placed his left hand horizontally and palm-upward upon his lap.
Each and every Tathāgata is surrounded by Vajradhara and other great Bodhisattvas.

One should then direct one’s own body and mind to serve and make offerings before each of these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, one should visualize that from within each of one’s bodies emerge immeasurable, exquisite incense, flowers, and various ritual implements; one should further imagine one’s own body becoming a vajra-throne and so forth, offering it to them, causing the eyes of the mind to see it with perfect clarity, as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas accept these offerings.
At that time, while in samādhi, the practitioner makes this vow:
"May all Tathāgatas and Vajrasattvas protect me; may they empower my body with this vajra-samādhi, namely, the syllable HŪṂ."
If one can enter in this manner, one will swiftly attain the Vajra Samantabhadra Samādhi.

Regarding the second stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, place the vajra-palms at the heart, face south, and [recite] the mantra up until 'grant me consecration,'" and so forth.
The commentary states:

Regarding its secret meaning, one should join the hands in the vajra-gesture and take refuge with single-minded devotion, visualizing that in the southern direction, throughout the entire realm of space, there is a world-system adorned solely with exquisite jewels, named the World-System of the Treasury of Jewel Radiance (*Ratnārciṣmatigarbha*).
Within it, Tathāgatas pervade the world in numbers equal to the atoms of all worlds.

At each Buddha’s location, one should imagine them surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, such as the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and Ratnaketu; all these Tathāgatas have entered the *ratnaprabhāsa-samādhi*.

As for the so-called full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*): one raises the right hand above the navel with the palm facing outward, manifesting the mark of a wondrous jewel within that palm; the left hand is placed horizontally and upward-facing upon the crossed legs.
The palaces where they dwell are all adorned with great jewels; the various bodhisattvas each hold jeweled banners and diverse precious offerings, all clearly and distinctly visible.
Furthermore, one should cultivate the visualization of offering one’s own body and so forth, exactly as previously described.
At that time, while within samādhi, he made this vow:
"May all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas such as Vajraratna bestow the empowerment of the Jewel Samādhi upon the crown of my head."

At that time, one should immediately visualize the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, all simultaneously conferring empowerment with the light of the nature of jewels; thus, the practitioner shall at once fulfill the stage of empowerment.
Do not harbor this thought:
"I am but an ordinary person; how could I possibly be at the stage of consecration for the bodhisattvas? Why is this?
Because it is of one nature with the *Ratnaprabhāsa-samādhi* and other such states.

Regarding the stage of the third turning of the wheel of Dharma, the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, placing the vajra-palms upon the head and [reciting] the mantra... even for me, turn the Vajradharmacakra," and so forth.
The commentary states:

Regarding the secret meaning, one should join the palms in homage, single-mindedly facing west, and visualize that throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space in the western direction, it is adorned exclusively with pure and wondrous vajra-jewel lotuses.
Furthermore, one should visualize all the Tathāgatas, surrounded by a host of great Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī, preaching the Dharma.
One should imagine each of these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to be as numerous as the atoms within all world-systems.
Each Buddha sat cross-legged and entered into samādhi; the assembly of bodhisattvas each held a lotus flower, within which were clearly visible Dharma wheels, Dharma conchs, and other such objects.
Again, one should visualize oneself making offerings, serving, and so forth, as described above.
At that time, within the samādhi, one should make this vow:
"May all the Tathāgatas, Vajradharmapadmacakravartin Bodhisattva, and the others, bestow this samādhi upon the crown of my head by means of empowerment."
At that time, the practitioner shall immediately visualize the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others conferring empowerment through the light of the Dharma-wheel.
Upon entering this contemplation, one shall at once be invested with the rank of all Buddhas who turn the wheel of Dharma, and shall be able to turn all wheels of Dharma; do not give rise to doubt.

Regarding the fourth point, the activities of all Buddhas, the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, with vajra-pañjalī joined, one places them from the crown of the head down upon the heart, and recites the mantra... even unto 'act as my vajra-activity' and so forth."
The commentary states:

Regarding the secret meaning, with palms joined in homage to the One, one should mentally contemplate the various and wondrously adorned worlds of the northern direction throughout the entirety of the realm of space, which are embellished by various multicolored flower garlands, necklaces, music, songs of praise, and marvelous Buddha-activities.
Furthermore, one should visualize all Tathāgatas and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds, preaching the Dharma within a vast and great congregation.
One should further imagine oneself serving and making offerings to each and every Tathāgata, as described above.
At that time, within the samādhi, each of one’s body, speech, and mind should make this vow:

"May all the Tathāgatas, the Vajrakarma Bodhisattvas, and the rest of the assembly of bodhisattvas, with their various karmic activities and the light of Buddha-wisdom, confer empowerment upon the crown of my head."

At that time, one should visualize the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others conferring empowerment through this radiance. When the practitioner enters this contemplation, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Functional Activity of Buddha-Wisdom Radiance, whereby they are able to extensively perform Buddha-deeds throughout the ten directions in a single thought-moment and at a single instant.
The sequence is as previously stated and as clarified in the extensive sūtras.
Because this sūtra is concise, I have described it here according to its essential meaning.

One should know that entry into this dharma-gate is extremely difficult; if one abides in the first direction or any of the other three directions, whichever direction is predominant, all other directions will be inferior.
If one enters the Tathāgata family, all is perfected simultaneously, with no distinction of superior or inferior. As the verse says:

"The four types of ritual procedures according to one's inclination, excluding the rites of increase, subjugation, and destruction. The Sūtra states: "Having performed the aforementioned rites of prostration toward the four directions, one may act according to the practitioner's desire; even a great Bodhisattva may sit in the half-lotus posture as they please," and so forth.
The commentary states:
This section contains four types of differentiated dharmas, which shall now be analyzed in detail.

The first is for the purpose of eliminating calamities; that is to say, when a practitioner cultivates merit, they are frequently obstructed and harassed by malevolent spirits and ghosts, causing their meritorious deeds and virtuous karma to be destroyed and fail to be accomplished.
When desire is intense, one should establish the practice by performing homa and other rites both before and after [the main rite].
Regarding the altar ritual: both the altar and the hearth are circular, and the seating arrangement is likewise; the appearance of the altar is white.
Seated upon a lotus throne, with a tranquil mind, one should recite the mantra.
For the firewood, use branches from a tree that are more than half-grown; they should be measured at ten finger-widths or eight finger-widths across and cut straight across.
For fuel, one may use sweet fruits such as plums, *vikaṅkata* wood (the identity of which is uncertain), and so forth; in short, any tree that bears sweet fruit may be used for this purpose.
For the fire, one may use fragrant flowers, white sandalwood, fragrant ghee, milk, parched grain flour, milk porridge, and sprouts of *kuśa* grass.
He was dressed in garments of grass.

As for the characteristics of his flames: first, red flames arose; next, they were like the color of gold; then, they were like molten gold or like the light of a lamp, changing colors from time to time.
Furthermore, if it is like the luster and moisture of the flame of cow-ghee, or like braided cords arranged in successive order—
should one possess such signs, it should be known that the vows sought through the ritual practice will all be accomplished.

Furthermore, as for the signs: when the fragrance is emitted profusely and the flames are intense yet soundless; or when there are layered flames atop the flames like reddish-gold; or when the tips of the flames disperse like the shape of a parasol—these are called the first sign.
Furthermore, regarding sound: it is like the sound of a cow, or sounds such as those of a conch shell, thunder, and so forth, as well as sounds that people delight to hear.
One should know that other various sounds, forms, and so on, are obstructive and cannot be accomplished [as objects of focus].

Regarding the second [type of] *vṛddhi* (augmentation): it refers to when a practitioner achieves *samādhi* and develops the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*). At that time, there are many internal obstacles; shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*) and obstructed by ignorance and darkness, one is unable to advance in practice. Even if one perseveres through diligent effort for a long period, the wisdom of the Buddha’s *bodhi* can ultimately not be attained. For this reason, one should perform the *vṛddhi-homa*.
The hearth and the ritual vessels should both be square and colored yellow.
One should sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) upon *kuśa* grass—this differs from the lotus seat mentioned elsewhere—and recite with a compassionate mind, looking about with joy.
One should perform the ritual using robes made of *kusha* grass and hemp.
As for the wood used for the fire, one should take the heartwood of a tree—branches that are thick and appear as if still living.

For the substances to be offered into the fire (*homa*), one should use ghee, milk, curd, honey, milk-gruel, curd-rice, sesame, rice grains, and the "three white foods," along with excellent yellow flowers, *nāgakesara* flowers, fragrances such as *tagara*, *śatapuṣpā*, *tianshen* (asparagus), and *vilva* fruit. These are to be employed to fuel the fire and perform the *homa*.
The firewood should be twelve finger-breadths long, cut with even ends.
The hearth should be one cubit deep, square in shape, and likewise in width;
it should be raised with four tiers of rims and plastered according to the ritual rules.
This recitation is the dharma of great vows for liberation and transcendence.
The signs of its accomplishment are as previously described, namely the first set of excellent marks and so forth.

Regarding the third, the method of subjugation: a practitioner on the path must possess majestic power; otherwise, it will be difficult to turn the wheel of Dharma, which those who have not been subdued find hard to love and take refuge in. Therefore, one should practice this *homa* rite.
Both the altar and the incense burner should be square and colored red.

One should sit with both knees folded together in the manner of the *bhadra-pīṭha* posture, or alternatively, one may squat as prescribed in the sūtras, ensuring that the buttocks do not touch the ground.
One should wear red garments;
with a heart full of exultation, one should recite the mantra.

As for the wood to be used, it must grow straight up from a single tree, rising above the other branches without any lateral growth; it should be measured at twelve finger-widths across and cut with a flat top.

Regarding the application of substances that yield milk, these refer to species such as the *sāṅgu* tree; furthermore, one should use milk, curd, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), honey, and the "three white foods," as well as seeds of the seven grains, sesame, rice, and the like. For the purpose of the fire ritual, one should employ red sandalwood incense, red flowers, storax (*sūkṣma*), frankincense (*guggulu*), and bdellium (*silha*).
Its characteristics are as described above.

Furthermore, it is said that wood unsuitable for use—such as trees that are withered and dry at the top, stripped of bark, short, crooked, or emaciated; wood that has been stripped of its bark, or is too long or too coarse, or has ever been cut by an axe, or possesses sores and diseases—is all unfit for use. However, if one is performing the fourth rite, such wood may be employed.

Furthermore, it is said that the evil characteristics of fire above are as follows: its heat is cold and it lacks a lustrous color; sparks fly out and its flames are like smoke, or the flames shoot into the ashes; furthermore, it emits a foul odor or is without smoke or flame; and the flames, mixed with embers, rise up and then sink back into the earth.

If one possesses these signs, it should be known that there are obstacles from internal or external humans and spirits, or that various hindrances such as afflictions and karma have not been extinguished.
One who encounters these signs must necessarily reform their practice and perform the aforementioned initial dharmas.
If one performs the fourth rite and attains this sign, it is called "accomplishment," because it accords with unwholesome dharmas.
Regarding this fourth rite of destruction, some may ask:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess great compassion; why do they teach sentient beings to perform such evil dharmas?"
Answer:
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who expound this Dharma do so for the sake of the wise, not for the foolish. Why is this?

Because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be many wicked people who, relying on their great power, follow false paths; they will disbelieve the True Dharma, destroy the signs of the Three Jewels that sustain it, and cause all sentient beings to lose the eye of Nirvana.
How pitiable and lamentable! This is governed by such a law.
For a Bodhisattva who practices this Dharma for the sake of benefiting others, there is great merit.

Yet, if one carefully observes that no benefit exists and instead gives rise to an evil mind to harm sentient beings, one incurs a grave and heavy offense; this is what the Buddha has prohibited and does not permit one to do arbitrarily.

If a person cultivates samādhi, remaining far removed from clamor and with a mind constantly tranquil, they contemplate the nature and characteristics of the Triple Gem as eternally abiding. Dwelling in the state of samādhi, they enter the realm of the Buddha; accomplishing wisdom, they perform great buddha-work, whereby the method of destruction is spontaneously accomplished.
As for this rite, both the altar and the hearth are entirely black, and it is performed within a triangle.
All the incense and flowers used are foul-smelling and black.

For fuel, one uses thorny wood with crooked branches; the dung of branchless, miserable camels and mules growing from tree roots is used as incense, mixed with the soil of the hearth to serve as the sacrificial food for the fire.
Use white mustard seed oil or fat and blood as lamp fuel.
Use bones, hair, or coffin wood, seven to six finger-widths long, with the tips cut off.
Clad in black garments or blood-stained robes,
one should crouch in a wrathful posture as described in the sūtras.
When performing the fire sacrifice and these malevolent signs appear, the rite is accomplished.
Furthermore, according to the *Yogācāra-mahāguhyatantra*, it is taught that there are twenty aspects of the secret fire ritual (*guhyāgnividhi*). What are these twenty?
These twenty kinds arise from three methods, namely: first, śāntika; second, pauṣṭika; and third, ābhicāruka.
To be able to eliminate all sins and perfect all merits, with a body that is tranquil and indestructible—this is called *śāntika* (the rite of pacification); herein lie four dharmas.

To swiftly accomplish all vows, to increase wealth, lifespan, and so forth, to be self-subdued in every way, for all who see one to hold them in reverent mindfulness, to possess various marks of physical excellence, to travel through the void of space, and to achieve mastery over realgar and other substances—this is called *pauṣṭika* (the rite of enrichment); herein lie nine dharmas.
Binding, subduing, destroying, and so forth—subjugating all obstacles, taming enemies and malevolent spirits—these are called the seven dharmas of Abhicāra.
These are called the twenty kinds of homa rituals; herein, there are further one hundred and ten kinds of fire rituals which are kept secret and not translated—this should be known.
Furthermore, the characteristics of twenty kinds of hearths are explained.
If one wishes to gather all beings, one should fashion the form of a vajra within the hearth.
If one wishes to subdue wicked people and the like, one should fashion the form of a lotus within the hearth.
If one wishes to eliminate all sins, the hearth should be made circular; it must have a gate, and the form of a jewel should be fashioned within the hearth, and likewise at the gate.
If one wishes for the increase of one's lineage, one should form the *karmamudrā* within the hearth, which is in the shape of a trident with a cross.
If it is for the sake of longevity, physical strength, and vitality, one should place a *kavaca* (armor) within the hearth, surrounding it with walls, moats, and the like.
If one wishes to accumulate all manner of wealth and goods, one should fashion a tooth-mark seal (daṃṣṭrā-mudrā) within the hearth.

If one desires all that is auspicious and excellent, and seeks peace and happiness in every place, one should place a wheel-shaped seal within the hearth, resembling the rim of a chariot wheel; the four sides of the hearth should also be in the shape of a wheel.
In this manner, the twenty kinds of seals (mudrā) are placed in sequence, as with the seals of the subsequent mandalas.
Alternatively, various seals may be placed according to the specific accomplishment (*siddhi*) sought.

Furthermore, regarding the decorative features outside the hearth (*kuṇḍa*): first, the hearth is measured at four cubits using a cord; the boundary paths and colored ground are established on its four sides, whether square, circular, or lotus-shaped, with all four faces level and upright.

The four gates serve as successive steps; the eight divisions of each gate are marked with lattice patterns and crescent shapes, and at the points where the steps approach the gates, one should draw the forms of Vajrayakṣas according to the ritual rules.

Outside the hearth, on the eastern side, draw the *svastika*, the Hu-xuanzi (whirling dancer), the water jar, the deer skin, and so forth; on the southern side, draw the conch shell, the crescent moon, the blade, the horse, the lion, the wild boar, and so forth; on the western side, draw the half-moon shape, the *mukuta* (wondrous hair-knot) mudrā, the bull banner mudrā, and so forth; on the northern side, draw the bronze gong, the banner, the peacock, the sheep, the rooster, and so forth.

Furthermore, the four gates are adorned with vajra seals and so forth: at the eastern gate is installed the Vajratāpana seal; at the southern gate, the Vajraratna seal; at the western gate, the Vajrapadma seal; and at the northern gate, the Vajrahūṃkāra seal.
Furthermore, place the sixteen great mudrās and so forth.
Erect pillars at the four corners and adorn them with flowering trees.
Arrange everything according to the ritual rules and make offerings to the Buddha.
The Buddha’s Great Method of Vajra-Wisdom is capable of eliminating all evils; whoever beholds it shall extinguish all transgressions.

When performing this rite, one should visualize oneself as Avalokiteśvara or Vajrapāṇi. Furthermore, one should visualize oneself wearing a crown, within which reside a Buddha and a vajra, or else jewels according to the specific ritual manual, thereby making the mind firm and steadfast.
Avalokiteśvara is the pure and wondrous Dharma-body wisdom of all Buddhas.
Vajrapāṇi is the firm bodhicitta of all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas.
One should paint it with the great forms of the pure precepts of the Buddhas of the six *pāramitās*.
In conjunction with the purification of the six sense faculties, one faces the east and performs the aforementioned rite; this is called the most supreme *śāntika* rite for the Buddha-bodhi.
The contemplation of the remaining dharmas may be understood by analogy.
If it is a pauṣṭika rite, employ the Vajraratna method.
If it is an ābhicāruka rite, employ the Vajrakrodha method.
Furthermore, one gathers all dharmas by means of the Vajra Armor [mudrā]. One grants long life and physical strength to the practitioner by means of the Vajra Longevity Medicine Seal.

One accumulates all wealth and goods by means of the Vajra Auspiciousness Seal. One protects the body by means of the Vajra Armor Seal. One travels through the air by means of the Vajra Accomplishment Seal. One accomplishes all wealth and goods by means of the Great Lotus Medicine Seal. One accomplishes all dharma-maṇḍalas by means of the Vajra Maṇḍala Seal. One accomplishes all auspiciousness by means of the Vajra King Seal.
Holding the seal with the left hand, one should burn fire with the right hand.
Furthermore, if one desires the increase of one's household, one should burn firewood made of sweet-scented wood along with non-glutinous rice.
If one desires the perfection of all requisites, one should burn seven grains of cereal or the seven precious gems mixed together.
If one desires supreme protection, one should burn sweet-smelling wood and stalks of *kuśa* grass smeared with oil.

If one desires long life, one should burn sweet wood, *kuru* grass, ghee, and fruits, while forming the *vajradaṇḍa-mudrā* with the left hand and holding it, and performing the fire-offering with the right hand.
If one wishes to subdue wicked people, one should burn bitter thorny needles, white mustard seeds, and earth from a wall;
if one burns vinegar, bitter fruits, and the like, all enemies will depart to a great distance.
If you wish for all to take refuge in faith and submit to you, burn red sandalwood and red flowers.
If you wish for those you command to follow your orders and not dare to disobey, use bitter thorn wood and perform the rite while maintaining an intensely wrathful visualization.
If one wishes to accomplish the grasping of all dharmas, burn white mustard seeds in the fire; one will immediately attain the most supreme auspiciousness.
The above concludes the method for purifying karmic obstructions and attaining inner and outer radiance.
Next follows the second [section]: the Dharma of the Seal of Wisdom on the True Reality of the Buddhas’ Sphere, which is the Samādhi of Entering Wisdom.
It is expressed in verse as follows:
To purify the desires of oneself and others, And further to eliminate the methods for defilements and obscurations.
Next, enter samādhi; with a firm mind, [apply] the dharmas of supernormal knowledge and wisdom.
First maintain the samaya, then bind the dharma of firm wisdom.
[One sees] the dharma and supreme joy; the syllable is the dharma-gateway of wisdom.
The secret seal opens the palace of the heart, Gathering one into the dharma of bodhi;
The wisdom seal is the syllable of the dharmakāya, The firm and stable dharma of bodhi.
The mantra of the great-power secret seal Protects the body and destroys obstacles.

Binding the Lotus Samādhi, according to the ritual of the honored deity of the Family of Delight (*Ratnakula*), one should visualize the seed-syllable of wisdom as the basis for the rite of adorning the assembly of Buddhas.

Regarding the first verse, which states, "The purification of oneself and others," the Sūtra says: "The practitioner desires that both themselves and the mantra be purified, and even their very nature be purified."
The commentary states:
The meaning of the prose sūtra can be understood through its literal sense.
As for the secret meaning: first, by contemplating the nature of the purity of the Buddha’s body of merit (*guṇakāya*), one realizes that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is pure.

Because one realizes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, this entirely pure dharmatā enters into my body; I am identical with the dharmatā, and therefore I am pure—the rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the verse’s phrase “also removing the dharma of defiled obstructions,” the Sūtra states: “Furthermore, one should contemplate these sentient beings, as well as the mantras, and even the cessation of mental activity and its objects of focus, so that they do not become distracted.”
The commentary states:
Regarding these three sections herein,
the prose of the first section is easily understood.

Regarding its secret meaning: the treasury of the Buddha’s wisdom and virtues has been individually accomplished by all Tathāgatas; all classes of sentient beings likewise possess this treasury and have accomplished it. Furthermore, [the Buddhas] equally vow to universally establish it for all as a source of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), so that all sentient beings may attain liberation. Therefore, it is said: "By performing such contemplation, one can eliminate all obstacles," and so forth.
The two sūtras state: "Furthermore, one should think: 'Whatever constitutes an obstruction, even down to the recollection of the bodhicitta,' and so forth.
The commentary explains:
Although that which is entangled by the three impurities is truly difficult to sever, through the single moment of union with the Buddha’s wisdom and bodhi, it is immediately extinguished.
The Bodhicitta is extensively praised in such works as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

What is taught in this scripture is that through direct entry, direct cultivation, direct fulfillment, and direct realization, one attains the stage of the Tathāgata in this very life by virtue of skillful wisdom.
The three sutras state: "Furthermore, all sentient beings in the world, up to those of immeasurable distinctions," and so forth.

The commentary explains: Sentient beings are perfumed by deluded karma and shrouded by the net of error; thus, upon seeing a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they instead perceive them as an adversary, and upon hearing the nectar-like Dharma, slander and resentment arise together. They create various kinds of evil karma and undergo various kinds of suffering bodies, just as a skilled artisan can produce myriad forms; yet, having created them themselves, they fear them themselves, unaware that they have brought this about themselves.
Because there are so many such [distractions], it is said that they consist of "various kinds of conceptual constructions and crafts, resulting in immeasurable distinctions.
Regarding the verse line "Next, one enters samādhi," the Sūtra says: "Seeing that sentient beings have such faults... and so forth, up to 'do not allow them to become distracted,'" and so on.
The commentary states: The remaining text is easily understood.

Regarding the term *apavijñānaka* mentioned here: *apa-* means "without"; *vijñānaka* refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*); *samādhi* means "equilibrium" or "even maintenance"; and *kāya* means "body. Thus, it should be rendered as "the equilibrium-maintenance of the body without consciousness."
One who enters this samādhi can counteract obstacles such as distractedness and discursive clinging; therefore, it is said that one should not move the mind or the limbs and joints of the body.
The lips and teeth are both closed, and the two eyes appear closed; one should quiet the mind’s clinging to objects so as not to allow it to become distracted.
Question:
What benefit is there for one who enters this meditative absorption? Answer:

If internal consciousness is distracted and drawn by external objects, consciousness follows those objects to give rise to various false perceptions; as soon as these perceptions arise and are followed by thoughts, one becomes entangled and bound by immeasurable defilements. Due to these causes and conditions, one sinks into the cycle of birth and death; therefore, one uses this samādhi to bring them to rest.
He asked again:
"This samādhi merely causes consciousness to cease and does not harmonize with worldly objects.

It is like the realm of the Buddhas—the supramundane true reality (*dharmatā*)—consisting of hundreds of thousands of samādhis, wherein one enters and emerges with mastery whether moving or unmoving; entering existence yet not existing, entering non-existence yet not non-existent; existence and non-existence are eternally one, and the one is immeasurable while the immeasurable is one. Furthermore, it establishes a blazing vastness, dwelling perpetually therein without obstruction or submergence."
Regarding how one attains such superior and wondrous merits through the application of this wisdom, as well as the practices for the benefit of oneself and others:

the answer is that one gradually studies the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna through the aforementioned gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Furthermore, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) likewise rely on these same concentrations; however, the Hīnayāna regards them as ultimate, whereas the non-Buddhists do not regard them as profound, each having their own distinct differences.
For those who gradually study the Mahāyāna, this serves as a skillful means for the purpose of ceasing攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective clinging).

However, for those who enter [the path] instantaneously, they do not rely on this, because all sensory objects of form are the activities of the Buddha, because the realm of formal characteristics is transformed by wisdom, and because the nature of wisdom possesses unimpeded and immeasurable function.
If one fears the realm of sensory objects and delights in emptiness and stillness, wisdom becomes useless; this is the deep net of the foolish and the clumsy.
Of such types there are many, some becoming śrāvakas and others becoming non-Buddhists. Alas! How pitiable and deeply regrettable!
Therefore, the Buddha has said that this gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, such that it cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Should one wish to enter it, it must be as extensively proclaimed in the subsequent sutra.

Regarding the verse line "The Dharma of firm resolve, penetration, and wisdom," the Sūtra states: "One should contemplate with clarity that the immeasurable Buddhas, mantras, and so forth, in the void, are eternally accordant," and so on.
The commentary states:
One who wishes to enter the gateway of wisdom should contemplate the characteristics of wisdom; one who wishes to accomplish the function of wisdom should apply it to the seeds of wisdom.
Therefore, looking up, one contemplates the empowerment of the Buddhas' bodies by means of the syllable Oṃ; the syllable Oṃ is the treasury of the Buddha's virtues.

Furthermore, by placing the syllable MAṬA upon the eyes, one causes the light of wisdom to arise; because this light of wisdom arises, one is praised by all Buddhas, and thus it is said that one "constantly attains accordance" and so forth.
This can be understood therein.
As for the secret meaning of the empowerment mantra, it is the wisdom-eye of the Buddha’s virtue-vajra-samādhi.
By means of this samādhi, one penetrates the gateway of wisdom, enabling wisdom to achieve internal and external harmony; who would not be subdued by such power?
Who would not comply?
Therefore, even things such as *siddhiya* can attain compliance.
*Siddhiya* refers to insentient objects and the like.
This name is kept secret and therefore not explicitly revealed.

Regarding the verse’s reference to "first maintaining the samaya," the Sūtra states: "Having performed this rite, one immediately forms the samaya-mudrā and recites the mantra... this is called the 'Vajra-joined palms' (vajra-añjali)," and so forth.
The commentary states:

The reason for forming this seal of illumination is that one’s own vessel of wisdom is opened and developed, becoming equal in radiance to the Buddha-wisdom; thus, self and other are harmoniously united as a single flavor without duality.
This clarifies that the mudrās can bring about union.
As for its secret meaning, it is called the "Union of the Buddha-Virtue Vajra Samādhi.
The characteristics of these mudrās are to be understood as they are explained in the sūtra.
Regarding the verse, "Next, bind the Firm Wisdom," the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, this very mudrā [accomplishes] all the perfections to their source, as well as the mantras," and so forth.
The commentary explains:

This clarifies that the mudrā is able to accomplish the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*); although wisdom is already in a state of union, it should be brought to full accomplishment, and for this reason, one empowers it with this [mudrā].
The "secret meaning" refers to the firm binding of the vajra-samādhi, intended so that accomplishment may be unbreakable.

Regarding the verse "seeing the dharmas and supreme joy," the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, it is like the vajra-binding and the mantras, up to the secret seals of the sons of the Buddha, and so forth."
The commentary states:
The Buddha’s self and wisdom are united.

Having further firmly established the palace of the *dharmadhātu*, which is perfect in its intrinsic nature, one manifests it by means of the *vidyā-mudrā*. Through the power of the *vidyā-mudrā*, one perceives the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); this is called the *vidyā* of the *Dharmasamayamudrā*.
Regarding its secret meaning: *samaya* means *samādhi*, because it equally induces [realization] so that one may see clearly.
*Sattva* (the three-syllable compound) means "entering me" and "I entering [it]," because they are of a single nature; all subsequent instances should be understood accordingly.
The Buddha bestows this luminous seal (*mudrā*) upon sentient beings through empowerment, enabling them to attain awakening; therefore, they are called "sons of the Buddha.
Regarding the verse "seeing the Dharma and supreme joy," the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, having bound the seal of supreme joy and the mantra, until it passes through like a needle," and so forth.
The commentary states:

Because one clearly perceives through the aforementioned empowerment that the nature of gnosis is without equal, and by recollecting and maintaining this rarity, one enters the Samādhi of Supreme Joy; one then employs empowerment by means of the vidyā-seal, and is therefore called the Samaya of Supreme Joy.
Regarding the secret meaning: *sattva* (the three syllables joined) means "I enter, I enter into me.
*Rakṣa* means "joyful exultation.
*Sulabha* means "supremely wondrous."
*Samaya* means meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
It refers to the supreme, wondrous joy of entering into oneself through equipoise and of oneself entering into that [object].
By the empowerment of the Buddha, it is sealed by the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*).
The mudrās are to be understood as explained in the sūtra.

Regarding the verse line “the syllable is the gateway to the dharmas of wisdom,” the sūtra states: “Furthermore, one binds the Vajrabandha mudrā, and so forth, until it becomes the gateway to the heart,” and so on.
The commentary states:

By means of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, which is firm, luminous, and boundless, one shall adorn one’s virtues; since nothing can proceed without a gateway, the syllable *traṭ* is taken as the heart-gateway.

The nature of the syllables is the essence of jewels, and light constitutes their gateway. If one wishes to open it, one applies the wisdom-seal (*jñāna-mudrā*); therefore, one immediately binds the gateway-opening seal.

Regarding the verse "The secret seal opens the dharma of the mind," the Sūtra states: "Recite this secret mantra three times upon the *samādhi* of the mind and the *mantra*, up until [the manifestation of] great celestial palaces," and so forth.
The commentary states:
The characteristics of the seals (*mudrā*) are easy to understand.
As for their secret meaning: the seal of the adamantine wisdom of the Buddha’s virtues can open the gate to the jewels of knowledge.
*Tralaṭa* refers to the jewel gate. Regarding the verse on "entering the dharma of bodhi," the sūtra states:
"Furthermore, visualize that before you is the syllable *Aṃ*, as well as the mantra and even the meaning of its phrases, all of which one realizes through self-awakening," and so forth.
The commentary states:

Once the gateway of wisdom has been opened, one should adorn the virtue of wisdom; this immediately incorporates the seed of bodhi, which is the syllable *Aṃ*. Therefore, it is said that one should contemplate with clarity that the syllable is entirely pervaded by brilliant, radiant, and dazzling light.
By contemplating with focused concentration, one shall cause [the deity] to enter; therefore, it is called the "Vajra Summoning and Entry Mudrā.
By the power of this mudrā, the Buddha’s virtue and bodhi abide within the palace of the mind.

Having thus become firmly established, one perceives with perfect clarity, like the lunar disc universally illuminating the *dharmadhātu*; this is called the mark of the Bodhi of Wisdom-Virtue (*jñānaguṇa-bodhi*).
Its secret meaning is that the seed of Bodhi is established within the Vajra-samādhi of the Buddha’s virtues.
This means that one clearly perceives the syllable *Aṃ* transforming into a moon disc and abiding within the palace of the mind.
Its mudrā is as clarified in the sūtra.
Because the wisdom-virtue of bodhi abides within the mind, it is said that one can comprehend the past, future, and present, and so forth, up to "all are realized through self-awakening," and so on.

Regarding the verse which states, “The wisdom-seal of the dharmakāya syllable is the firm dharma of bodhi,” the sūtra says: “Furthermore, by forming the vajra-fist and the seal-mudrā, and so forth, up to the secret of mind, because it is capable of grasping and maintaining [the essence], it is called the ‘vajra-fist,’ and so on.”
The commentary states:
The method of the seal-marks (*mudrā*) is easy to understand.

As for its secret meaning, it refers to the Dharma-realm wisdom-seal (*dharmadhātu-jñāna-mudrā*) of the Buddha-virtue Vajra-samādhi; by sealing [all phenomena] with this seal, through the power of that seal, one is able to accomplish the Dharma-realm Bodhi-body (*bodhi-kāya*).
The syllable *Ṭha* is the seed-syllable of the Dharma-realm; its form resembles a circular stupa and is called the "Dharmakāya Stupa.
The "Vajra Fist" is the mark of the Buddha’s firm wisdom.

By means of the Buddha’s firm wisdom, one upholds the Dharmakāya; this seal of wisdom and bodhi can cause the treasury of firm virtues to be accomplished. Therefore, it is called the "Sealed Heart-Palace," and is further named the "Vajra Fist," and so forth.

Regarding the verse, "Protecting the body and subduing obstacles by means of the Great Power Mudrā and Mantra," the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, divide the vajra-fist into two, [recite] the mantra, and so forth, until all are rendered pure."
The commentary states:
This refers to having first purified body and speech, and subsequently abiding in firm wisdom.
Furthermore, because it is conjoined with bodhi, the treasury of virtues is fully perfected.
To increase the power of the Vidyārāja for protecting the body and subduing obstacles, it is said, "With this mudrā, rotate it clockwise upon the head," as can be understood from the sūtra.

Regarding the verse, "One should immediately bind the samaya [mudrā] according to the dharma of the chosen Family Lord," the sūtra states, "Furthermore, one binds the vajra-lotus and the mantra, and so forth, until one attains the status of a Lord."
The commentary states:

Having performed the aforementioned binding and protection, one should, according to one's preference, place the Samaya-mudrā of the Family Lord at the heart or the crown; thereafter, one should recite the mantra of that particular family.
In the sūtra, only the samaya-mantra and mudrā of the Padma family are present; those of the other four families are not mentioned because they were omitted for the sake of brevity.
If one wishes to understand them, it is simply a matter of changing the word *padma* and substituting the words *vajra*, *ratna*, *karma*, and *dharmadhātu*. Thus it is.
The remaining phrases are all the same; they may be understood through reflection.
The mudrās should also be modified according to each phrase, as their characteristics are explained in detail in the text below.

If one desires to extensively observe the Tathāgata’s Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Adornments of the True Nature (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), one should establish and carefully observe it according to the sequence provided hereafter.
Within this gateway of wondrous adornment, the assembly of Buddhas is established based upon the seeds of wisdom.
Thus, it is said in verse:
"Wondrous wisdom purifies both the internal and external; It is established by relying upon the seeds."
The wondrous marks of the world’s dharmas, the objects of contemplation upon which all Buddhas rely,
the dharmas for attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, the signs of the Tathāgata’s supernormal transformations,
and the signs of secret samādhi.
Regarding the verse line "Sublime wisdom purifies the internal and external," the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, pure and sublime wisdom... even equaling empty space," and so forth.
The commentary explains:
The nature of the six sense objects and the six consciousnesses is emptiness as its essence; all that exists is entirely of one suchness.

Sentient beings harbor attachments within their minds that create obstructions; wishing to establish the sublime marks, one must first use wisdom to eliminate them. Therefore, it is said that one observes that both the internal and external are entirely non-existent.

Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is equal and devoid of beginning, middle, or end, it is said: "Furthermore, one contemplates that the phenomena of the three times are identical to empty space.

When entering this *śūnyatā-samādhi*, one perceives neither body nor mind; both internal and external are stilled, such that the subject who contemplates and the object contemplated are both identical to the single great emptiness.
If those of the śrāvaka lineage predominate, they remain submerged therein and their wisdom does not stir;
outsiders, however, give rise to evil seeking within it, perceiving either finitude, or infinity, or neither finitude nor infinity, and so forth, until various distinct views arise individually.
Within this state, the bodhisattva possesses skillful wisdom and establishes various subtle marks and functions; entering the realm of the Buddhas, they receive the Buddhas' empowerment.

By virtue of this empowerment, they enter and emerge from hundreds of thousands of samādhis without obstruction, and are able to go everywhere to the great assemblies of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas to make offerings, prostrate, and inquire about the meaning of the Dharma, yet their body and mind remain unmoving and unabsorbed.
They are likewise able to enter universally into the realms of sentient beings to teach and transform inexhaustible classes of beings, yet their body and mind remain unattached and unimpeded.

If one who practices correctly with such an uninterrupted mind can, for a single thought-moment and at a single time, be equal to the Tathāgata without before or after, they shall fulfill the stage of Buddhahood in this very life.
The ritual procedure is as explained below; perform it according to your preference.

Regarding the verse, "Establishing the World’s Wondrous Features based on Seeds," the Sūtra states: "One should visualize the syllable *YAM* beneath [the central seat], and so forth, until one has visualized the seats for all the aforementioned divisions."
The commentary states:

Having thus entered the *samādhi* of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), one then uses decisive, sublime wisdom to visualize the syllable *YAM* at the limit of space below; black light radiates forth and transforms into a wind-wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
The wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala), possessing great power, supports the earth-circle (pṛthivī-maṇḍala); these circles are all black in color, and this is called the element of wind and earth.
Herein, the establishment of the world differs from that in the Vairocana Sūtra; one should practice fully according to what is taught therein.

Having performed the visualization as before, one arranges the syllable *khaṃ* along the perimeter of the earth-circle; it emits light of various colors, forming the Cakravāḍa Mountains, which are called the "Coast of the Nectar of Immortality."

With the syllable *BHRŪṂ*, the seed-syllable of the dharma-realm, which is great white in color and emits rays of compassionate light, one should visualize the Tathāgata Vairocana in the midst of space; this is called the "seed of the dharmakāya" and has the characteristic of raining down, as described in the sūtra.
Visualize the syllable *praḥ*; from this syllable, golden light is emitted, which transforms into a golden tortoise—vast and boundless, the seed of auspiciousness.
Visualize the syllable *hrīḥ*; it emits yellow light and becomes a golden lotus, the seed of the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*). Its characteristics are as described in the sūtra.

One should visualize the three syllables *Bhram* (pronounced *pra*), *Hūṃ*, and *Jraḥ*, which emit light of various jewel colors, forming Mount Meru (formerly called Miaogao, "Wonderfully High"), the seed-syllable of the firm and supreme Dharma-realm seat; its characteristics are as described in the sūtra.

That which people today commonly call the "Sumeru Seat" derives its name from this; it is not the Mount Sumeru composed of the four jewels. Because this wondrous seat is lofty and prominent like that mountain, it is thus metaphorically described.

The mountain has eight faces, each with its own gate; within it is a vast, uniform space, the palace where the eight great bodhisattvas constantly reside, and these bodhisattvas each occupy one face while expounding the Dharma.

Within that inner chamber, there is a great assembly of Buddhas from the ten directions as numerous as atoms; this scripture does not list them in detail for the sake of brevity, but the sequence of the Tripiṭaka teachings establishes them in full, which is why it says "there are eight faces," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the visualization of the five syllables, *vaṃ* and so forth: this means that these five syllables are arranged upon the pedestal according to their respective positions.

The light rays emitted by these five syllables merge together to form a great four-sided palace. Within this great palace, according to the positions of the syllables, five-peaked pavilions are manifested; this is called the Great Palace of Five Peaks.
The adornments therein are as extensively explained in the Sūtra, including even the kings of the *mahoragas* performing exquisite songs and dances.

Beneath each pavilion, according to the positions of the five syllables, there are formed vajra-wheel maṇḍalas and the like; within each wheel, there are three seed-syllables that serve as the Buddha-thrones, as clarified in the Sūtra.

Regarding the lion throne formed from the seed-syllable *vaṃ* within the wheel of syllables among the five seats: the lion is the king of all beasts, who wanders among all beasts without fear; likewise, Vairocana Buddha is the king of all dharmas, who manifests transformations among all dharmas without obstruction, and thus he occupies the lion throne.

Regarding the elephant seat transformed from the seed-syllable within the *hūṃ*-wheel: as for the power and function of that elephant, no other animal’s power can surpass it; its representation atop the King of the Vajra Family signifies firm strength that is unimpeded.

Regarding the horse-seat manifested from the seed-syllable within the *tla* syllable-circle: among all that is noble and auspicious in the world, none precedes the horse; the horse possesses the function of wisdom and is thus regarded as a treasure. The consecrated Dharma King takes it as his seat to signify that he is endowed with the auspiciousness of consecration.

Regarding the peacock throne transformed from the seed-syllable within the *hrīḥ* wheel: in the world, the peacock is regarded as an auspicious bird; its form is beautiful, endowed with various colors, and it possesses clear intelligence that accords well with the timing of the seasons. The Wheel-Turning King uses it as a seat to signify that he turns the Great Wheel of Dharma for those who are not unsuitable vessels.

Regarding the Garuḍa seat transformed from the seed-syllable within the *A*-syllable wheel: the power of this bird is able to subjugate all nāgas. Within the four great oceans where the nāgas dwell, wherever the Garuḍa bird directs its course, the nāgas are immediately subdued. King Amoghasiddhi takes this as his seat to symbolize the performance of *karma* (ritual action) in accordance with the directions through the application of wisdom, thereby gathering in humans, devas, and all nāgas.
"None do not return" means that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas gather and lead beings back according to their needs, and there is no one who does not comply.
One should understand this sequence deeply; therefore, it is said: "Having visualized the seats of the various assemblies as described above," and so forth.

Regarding the verse on "visualizing the dharmas upon which all Buddhas rely to achieve perfect enlightenment," the Sūtra states: "Next, visualize all Tathāgatas of the various families, as well as the sixteen great Bodhisattvas, up to the skillful means and wisdom of unimpeded activity," and so forth.

The commentary states: This passage of the sūtra is arranged out of sequence; it should rather be stated as follows: "One should visualize a moon disc upon each of the five types of lion thrones previously mentioned. Within each moon disc, one should visualize a subtle lotus pedestal with its filaments fully complete. Then, within the moon disc upon the lion throne, one should visualize the four-faced Vairocana Buddha, seated upon that throne with the bodies sustained by all the Tathāgatas."
Furthermore, one should visualize the Buddhas of the four directions, such as Akṣobhya and others, each occupying their respective seats,

along with the sixteen great bodhisattvas, the four goddesses of the pāramitās, the four types of internal offerings, the four types of external offerings, and the bodhisattvas of the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu).

Furthermore, the thousand Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, the great Vajras, and the various deities of the twenty-eight divisions, each, by means of their own samādhi, visualized their respective distinct mudrās and signs.
All these phenomena appear from within the circular light of the Dharmadhātu-body of Vairocana Buddha.

Thus, not long after the Tathāgatas such as Akṣobhya Buddha sat upon this [throne], they attained equal and perfect enlightenment and fully realized the Samantabhadra-mind of all Tathāgatas, up to and including the attainment of the wisdom of the four empowerments, as extensively described in the sūtras.
Regarding the initial statement, "Vairocana with four faces," the commentary explains:
it refers to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata within the wheel of the syllable *vaṃ*, who is perfectly complete with four faces and displays the *samādhi* mudrā toward the four directions.

Next, regarding the verse line "The marks of the Tathāgata’s spiritual transformations and the marks of the secret samādhi," this refers to all the subsequent sections: the Tathāgatas of the five directions, the sixteen bodhisattvas, the four pāramitās, the four internal and external offerings, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the various bodhisattvas. Each of these possesses infinite, profoundly deep gates of wisdom and application of wisdom—namely, the marks of the secret realm of unimpeded spiritual transformations and samādhi—as explained extensively below.
The first is the Samādhi Door of the Universal Worthy Vajra of All Tathāgatas.
The verse says:
